newsitem.title: UK: Saudi dissident threatens holy war against U.S..
newsitem.headline: Saudi dissident threatens holy war against U.S..

text.p: Exiled Saudi dissident and rebel leader Osama bin Laden threatened to wage an Islamic holy war against the United States and its allies if Washington does not remove its troops from the Gulf region.

In an interview from his headquarters in Afghanistan for the British documentary programme Dispatches to be broadcast on Thursday, bin Laden said the U.S. was occupying and violating Islam's greatest and holiest lands and must be expelled.
He said bombings in Riyadh in November 1995 and at a military housing complex in the eastern city of al-Khobar last June in which 24 Americans were killed were a warning to Washington.

"The bombings...were a clear indication for the crusading forces to correct this grave mistake and for them to depart before it is too late and before the battle begins in earnest," he said in the interview filmed by one of his followers.
"People will not only hit the American military but also demand the expulsion of American civilians."

"This war will not only be between the people of the two sacred mosques and the Americans but it will be between the Islamic world and the Americans and their allies because this war is a new crusade led by America against the Islamic nations."

Saudi Arabia is home to Islam's two most sacred shrines in the cities of Mecca and Medina. King Fahd, whom bin Laden has accused of running a corrupt state, considers himself Custodian of the Two Holy Shrines.
"To my knowledge this is the first filmed interview he has done," said independent film maker Gwynne Roberts who waited months to speak to bin Laden.
Roberts spoke to bin Laden at his Afghanistan headquarters guarded by the Taleban radical Islamic student militia who seized control of the Afghan capital Kabul last year.
Although Roberts met bin Laden and interviewed him, he was not allowed to record it. He later gave a camera and questions to one of the rebel leader's followers who returned with the film.
"What came back was not my interview. He was basically talking to his own followers."
The United States has described bin Laden, the son of a Saudi construction magnate, as one of the "most significant financial sponsors of Islamic extremist activities in the world".

Some Middle East experts estimate his fortune at $300 million. The U.S. State Department has linked the rebel leader, believed to be in his mid-40s, to guerrilla training camps in Afghanistan and Sudan and said he backed a bid to bomb U.S. forces in Yemen in 1992.
Roberts described bin Laden as a Messiah-type figure who wields enormous influence among his followers and was behind the Saudi bombings.

"He leads the Arab Afghan movement which is involved with Algeria, Egypt, Tunisia, Libya and throughout the Middle East. He is like a mentor for these people. The links obviously go throughout the Middle East and into central Asia," said Roberts.
